newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Smuggled oil squeezes market share in Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Smuggled oil squeezes market share in Taiwan.

text.p: Taiwan's private oil retailers are pressing the government to liberalise oil product imports ahead of schedule to protect diesel and gasoline sales being eroded by smugglers, industry sources said on Wednesday.
"There is a lot of smuggling because currently private firms are not allowed to import and taxes are very high," a Taiwanese oil trader told Reuters.
An official with state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC) smuggled products accounted for around 10 percent of the retail market. Traders put the figure much higher.
"Around a third of the T$400 billion ($14 billion) per year retail market is smuggled oil," said one.
Each month Taiwan consumes up to 85,000 barrels per day (bpd) of diesel and 126,000-bpd of gasoline, CPC sources said.
Taiwan imports up to 250,000 bpd of oil products, a CPC official said.
The bulk of smuggled oil is diesel, which is put on 2,000-to-3,000-tonne barges or disguised as other products, such as solvents, which are subject to lower taxes, the industry sources said.
The smuggled products are sold either through a large number of unlicensed gas stations or directly to large customers for use in trucks, power generators or small marine vessels.

"The diesel users are transportation companies which consume a lot and care more about the cost than the quality, so they have much interest to buy directly from smugglers," an industry source said. "Private car owners are more concerned with the
quality of gasoline."
He said smuggling had increased substantially over the past year. But a government task force set up to deal with the problem two months ago had begun to get a grip on the problem, the trader added..
The volume of smuggled oil could be exaggerated by private retailers who want the government to ease import regulations quickly, some officials said.
"There is big pressure from the public to liberalise imports," another CPC official said.
CPC has a monopoly over imports and supplies the diesel and gasoline to its own 560 stations and 700 private stations.
In June last year, Taiwan's Energy Commission allowed private oil imports by producers. But since CPC is the only refiner, it is the only qualified importer.
"The government has some timetable to liberalise the petroleum industry in two stages," a CPC official said.

The first stage in 1999 allows for free imports of aviation jet fuel, fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gas. Deregulation of all products, including diesel and gasoline, is expected some time in 2000 or 2002, he said.
"By the time the first stage is due, in the two to three years, maybe there will be some changes," the CPC official said. "There is still uncertainty with the time table."
CPC's monopoly is expected to end in early 1998 when Formosa Plastics commissions its naphtha cracker, the first phase of a US$9.0-billion refinery complex.
The cracking unit can produce 450,000-tonnes of ethylene and 230,000 tonnes of gasoline a year.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870 3086)
